description: Tackling the "Earth System Trend Detective" challenge to turn environmental data into impactful interactive visuals. I'm a Software Engineering student & Full-Stack Dev with an AI/ML foundation. Looking for teammates in Data/Earth Science (analyzing datasets), UI/UX (visualizing insights), and Storytelling/Research (crafting the pitch). Join us!
summary: Antarctic Ice Mass Trend Detective is an interactive 3D platform that uses NASA satellite data to investigate where, how much, and since when Antarctica is losing ice. By processing GRACE and GRACE-FO observations, our open-source pipeline analyzes monthly ice-mass changes across West Antarctica, East Antarctica, and the Antarctic Peninsula. We apply statistical methods to distinguish long-term trends from natural variability and identify when the evidence becomes statistically significant. Through interactive visualizations, 3D exploration, time-series charts, and a detection timeline, users can explore regional differences, uncertainties, and the influence of snowfall. The platform also connects Antarctic ice loss to projected sea-level rise in 17 coastal cities. By making complex scientific data accessible, transparent, and explorable, Trend Detective helps students, researchers, and the public understand how Antarctica is changing and why long-term satellite observations matter.
details:
Antarctic Ice Mass Trend Detective is a web-based interactive 3D expedition that answers one question about our planet: is Antarctica losing its ice, where, by how much, and since when can we say so with statistical confidence? Most reports give a single number for the whole continent. Our platform opens that number up, sector by sector and month by month, and adds the piece that is usually missing: the moment when the evidence became strong enough to rule out natural variability.

How it works:

Trend Detective ingests the NASA/JPL GRACE and GRACE Follow-On mascon solution (RL06.3 CRI, April 2002 to July 2026) and sums the ice-mass signal over the Antarctic drainage-system sectors defined by Zwally et al. (West, East, Peninsula). Each sector's monthly series is deseasonalised, its trend is estimated with Theil-Sen (95% confidence interval) and tested with Mann-Kendall using an effective sample size that corrects autocorrelation. An expanding window then finds the first year from which the trend stays statistically significant, and we compare that with the analytical years-to-detect of Weatherhead et al. (1998). NASA's MERRA-2 reanalysis puts snowfall variability in context, because snow is the main natural noise hiding the signal. A stress-test lab shows how the answers change with start date, mission gap and instrument splice.

What it finds (all computed from NASA data by our open pipeline):

- Antarctica as a whole: about −128 Gt/year, detectable since 2008.

- West Antarctica: about −160 Gt/year, detectable since 2016.

- Antarctic Peninsula: about −29 Gt/year, not yet detectable (roughly 17 years of record needed).

- East Antarctica: about +61 Gt/year, a gain, detectable since 2009.

Key Benefits & Impact:

- Shows scientists and students that "Antarctica is losing ice, but not everywhere", and how long a record must be before a trend can be trusted.

- Helps researchers prioritise sectors where the signal is still hidden in the noise.

- Connects the ice sheet to people: using IPCC AR6 projections, it shows how much of the sea-level rise at 17 coastal cities comes from Antarctica alone, across three emissions scenarios and four dates.

- Gives non-programmers visual, no-code access to a large satellite dataset, with uncertainty stated openly (including NASA's published ±39 Gt/year, which also covers the glacial isostatic adjustment model).

- Fully open: every number on the site comes from a tested pipeline in our public repository.

Tools & Technologies:

- Python (NumPy, SciPy, pandas, xarray, netCDF4) for preprocessing, trend statistics, sector masks and tests (pytest)

- React 19, TanStack Start and TypeScript for the web app, with Zod validating the data contract

- Three.js / React Three Fiber for the 3D globe and ice-sheet scenes, Recharts for the time series and detection charts

- Vitest for front-end tests, GitHub for collaboration, Vercel for hosting

- Data: NASA/JPL GRACE and GRACE-FO, NASA GMAO MERRA-2, IPCC AR6 sea-level projections, NASA Blue Marble

Creative Elements:

- A nine-chapter "expedition" from orbit to the ice sheet, built around the three questions of the challenge: where, how much, and since when.

- A hands-on "since when?" scrubber: the viewer drags an expanding window and watches the trend lock in against the snow noise.

- A heat map that follows the real continent outline, with live telemetry under the cursor.

- Everyday comparisons (tonnes of ice per second, school buses, a 16 m cube of ice) next to the sea-level conversion, so the numbers can be felt.

- A "cities nearest to me" option that makes sea-level rise personal; location is requested only after a click.

- Works with wheel, swipe or arrow keys, with sound off by default and reduced-motion support.

Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI)

We used AI tools to speed up development and documentation.

- AI-assisted code autocomplete and coding assistants helped write code, tests and documentation throughout the repository.

- An AI assistant (Claude code) helped us assemble the website: the interface, the 3D scenes, the charts and the data-processing scripts, always from our own data choices, method and design decisions. Everything was reviewed and edited by the team.

- Lovable.dev: To prototype page structure and layout faster.

- No NASA logos or branding were generated or imitated by AI.

AI helped accelerate the process, but the scientific question, the statistical method, the choice of datasets, the sector definitions and the interpretation of results were team-led. Every figure shown comes from NASA data processed by our own tested code.

Team Capivara Astronauta: Priscilla Leandro, Alexandre Moreira, Matheus Oliveira and Maria Eduarda Ishimaru.
